Glasco-144.remote_wikitext:
== Biography ==

'''Thomas Glascoe''' married [[Duffy-?|Margaret Duffy]], daughter of [[Duffy-?|Patrick Duffy]] and his wife Anne.

An undated handwritten pedigree of the Duffy family identifies Margaret as:

: “Margt, wife of Thomas Glascoe”

Margaret’s father, Patrick Duffy, was associated with Back Lane, Dublin. The pedigree states that Patrick made his will on 9 April 1774 and that it was proved in June 1775.

The pedigree also names Margaret’s siblings as John Duffy, Peter Duffy, Judith Duffy, Mary Duffy, and possibly Teresa Duffy. Judith married Cornelius Blewitt.

No children of Thomas and Margaret are shown on the pedigree. This does not prove that they had no children.

== Research Notes ==

* Thomas’s birth and death dates are unknown.
* His birthplace and residence are not stated.
* His occupation and parentage have not been identified.
* No marriage date or place has yet been found.
* The surname is written as '''Glascoe''' in the pedigree. Searches should also consider variants such as Glasco, Glascow and Glasgow.
* Thomas should not be assigned a Dublin birthplace solely because his father-in-law lived at Back Lane, Dublin.
* Patrick Duffy’s probate record may contain further information about Thomas and Margaret.

Glasgow-1024.public_addition_wikitext:
=== Possible James Glasco of Omagh ===
The 1786 marriage column names James Glasco, Omagh publican aged 61, and Jane Murray of the same place aged 16.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/1050075355/ The Public Register, or, Freeman's Journal, 1786-09-05, p.3].</ref>

Three 1793 Hope advertisements name James Glasco, Omagh, as a freight/passage contact; the 25 May issue adds a sailing delay.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/72021067/ The Northern Star, 1793-05-11, p.1].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/72021086/ The Northern Star, 1793-05-18, p.4].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/72021100/ The Northern Star, 1793-05-25, p.1].</ref>

The marriage was reported by 5 September 1786; the exact ceremony day is not given. James’s reported age suggests birth about 1724–1725. The same uncommon name and Omagh business context support, without proving, continuity with the 1793 contact. The notices do not name his parents or establish a previous marriage.

This may concern [[Glasgow-1024]]. Estimated birth c.1722 and Moneymore context are compatible; neither identifies the Omagh publican.

=== Possible James Glascow, Fogs Manor postal addressee ===
James Glascow, Fogs Manor, is listed among letters remaining in the Philadelphia post office.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/39395391/ The Pennsylvania Gazette, 1757-04-07, p.1].</ref>

Fogs Manor is the printed address qualifier. A neighbouring "Phil. Co." in a separate alphabetic column is not this man’s address. The list states no occupation, so it does not identify him as the later Greenwich Packet master.

This may concern [[Glasgow-1024]]. Estimated c.1722 birth is chronologically plausible; death date absent. Irish location is not a concrete contradiction. The postal record states no occupation.

=== Possible James Glascow, master of Greenwich Packet ===
Greenwich Packet: James Glascow, master; James Young, owner; from Philadelphia to Winyew, Carolina; with rum, bread, flour and porter.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/34421452/ The Public Advertiser, 1777-05-14, p.2].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/396765804/ The Ipswich Journal, 1777-05-17, p.1].</ref><ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/971522063/ The Gloucester Journal, 1777-05-19, p.1].</ref>

James Young is the separate vessel owner, not another form of the master’s name. Three issues repeat one voyage report. Neither the route nor the cargo establishes the master’s family or identifies him with the 1757 Fogs Manor addressee.

This may concern [[Glasgow-1024]]. Estimated c.1722 birth is chronologically plausible; death date absent. Irish location is not a concrete contradiction.

=== Possible James Glasgow, Edinburgh game certificate, 1789 ===
James Glasgow, Esq., Edinburgh, appears in the Mid-Lothian game-duty list of certificates issued since 8 September 1789.<ref>[https://www.newspapers.com/image/601822968/ The Edinburgh Advertiser, 1789-12-11, p.8].</ref>

The list gives an Edinburgh designation but no age or relatives; it is not evidence of a military or maritime career.

This may concern [[Glasgow-1024]]. Birth c.1722, estimated, County Londonderry; death date not recorded. Chronologically possible, but no Edinburgh/certificate connection is documented.

Glasgow-1150.remote_wikitext:
{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

== Biography ==

'''James Glasgow''' was born before 16 June 1641, probably in Scotland. His precise date and place of birth have not been identified.

He became a weaver and burgess of Edinburgh.

=== Apprenticeship and burgess status ===

On 16 June 1641 James, explicitly described as a son of '''Robert Glasgow, servant to William Crichtoun in Wester Duddingston''', was apprenticed to William Sclaitter, weaver.<ref name="Apprentice1641">Francis J. Grant, ed., ''Register of Apprentices of the City of Edinburgh, 1583–1666'' (Scottish Record Society, 1906), printed p. 71, [https://archive.org/details/scottishrecordso28scotuoft/page/71/mode/2up scan]: “Glasgow, James, son to Robert G., servitor to William Crichtoun, in Wester Duddingston, with William Sclaitter, weaver 16 June 1641.”</ref>

James was admitted as a burgess of Edinburgh on 20 June 1649. The entry identifies him as a weaver, states that he had been apprenticed to the deceased William Sklatter, and repeats the apprenticeship date of 16 June 1641.<ref name="Burgess1649">Charles B. Boog Watson, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/roll_of_edinburgh_burgesses_1406_to_1700.pdf#page=218 ''Roll of Edinburgh Burgesses and Guild-Brethren, 1406–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1929), printed p. 208: “Glasgow, James, B., weiver, as p. to umq. Wm. Sklaitter, weiver, B. (16 June 1641) 20 June 1649.”</ref>

The matching master and exact apprenticeship date establish that the 1641 apprentice was the later Edinburgh weaver and burgess.

=== Marriages ===

James married first '''[[Whyte-2772|Bessie Whyte]]''' at Edinburgh on 6 July 1649.<ref name="EdinburghMarriages">Henry Paton, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/register_of_marriages_for_the_parish_of_edinburgh_1595-1700_~_1898.pdf#page=277 ''Register of Marriages for the Parish of Edinburgh, 1595–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1905), printed p. 267: “Glasgow, James, weaver; Bessie Whyte 6 July 1649” and “James, weaver; Agnes Duncan 11 Nov. 1653.”</ref>

He married second '''[[Duncan-16106|Agnes Duncan]]''' at Edinburgh on 11 November 1653.<ref name="EdinburghMarriages" />

The matching name, occupation and parish, together with the sequential dates, identify the bridegroom in both entries as the same James Glasgow.

=== Children ===

James's known children were:

* '''[[Glasgow-3097|Helen Glasgow]]''', daughter of Bessie Whyte;
* '''[[Glasgow-3099|Jonet Glasgow]]''', daughter of Bessie Whyte;
* '''[[Glasgow-1374|Robert Glasgow]]''', son of Agnes Duncan;<ref name="RobertBaptism">“Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950,” database, ''FamilySearch'', [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VRSV-T1T Robert Glasgow, baptised 5 May 1655, Edinburgh], son of James Glasgow and Agnes Duncan.</ref>
* '''[[Glasgow-3143|Marion Glasgow]]''', daughter of Agnes Duncan;
* '''[[Glasgow-1373|Bethia Glasgow]]''', daughter of Agnes Duncan; and
* '''[[Glasgow-1057|John Glasgow]]''', son of Agnes Duncan.

The individual baptismal records should be consulted for the evidence identifying each child's mother.

Marion Glasgow married William Calder at Edinburgh on 29 June 1686.<ref name="MarionMarriage">Henry Paton, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/register_of_marriages_for_the_parish_of_edinburgh_1595-1700_~_1898.pdf#page=278 ''Register of Marriages for the Parish of Edinburgh, 1595–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1905), printed p. 268: “Glasgow, Marion; William Calder 29 June 1686.”</ref>

On the following day William Calder was admitted as a burgess through his wife Marion, who was explicitly described as a daughter of James Glasgow, weaver and burgess.<ref name="CalderBurgess">Charles B. Boog Watson, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/roll_of_edinburgh_burgesses_1406_to_1700.pdf#page=101 ''Roll of Edinburgh Burgesses and Guild-Brethren, 1406–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1929), printed p. 91: “Calder, Wm., B., weaver, be r. of w. Marion, dr. to James Glasgow, weaver, B. 30 June 1686.”</ref>

This directly establishes Marion as James's daughter.

James's date and place of death have not been identified.

== Research Notes ==

=== Birth ===

The former birth date of 19 March 1626 and birthplace of Inveresk do not belong to this James.

The only presently supported birth statement is that James was born before 16 June 1641, when he entered his apprenticeship.<ref name="Apprentice1641" />

His birthplace remains unknown.

=== Parentage ===

The apprenticeship record directly identifies James's father as '''Robert Glasgow, servant to William Crichtoun in Wester Duddingston'''.<ref name="Apprentice1641" />

'''[[Glasgow-1156|Robert Glasgow]]''' is a plausible existing-profile match for this father because of the Wester Duddingston association and chronology. The record does not, however, contain enough information to prove that the named father and the existing profile represent the same man. That relationship should therefore remain uncertain.

The record does not name James's mother.

'''[[Ivey-2264|Deborah Ivey]]''' is not identified as his mother in any inspected record. Any attachment should remain uncertain and be treated as a working hypothesis rather than an established relationship.

=== Distinct from the Inveresk James ===

This James was not '''[[Glasgow-3923|James Glasgow]]''', who was baptised at Inveresk and Musselburgh on 19 March 1626 as a son of [[Glasgow-1148|Alexander Glasgow]] and [[Clerk-296|Jannet Clerk]].<ref name="InvereskBaptism">“Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564–1950,” database, ''FamilySearch'', James Glasgow, baptised 19 March 1626, Inveresk and Musselburgh, son of Alexander Glasgow, [https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:VQ4V-GQW record VQ4V-GQW] (accessed 2025).</ref>

The 1641 apprenticeship names Robert Glasgow, not Alexander Glasgow, as the father of the Edinburgh weaver. The two men should remain on separate profiles.

=== Incorrect child profile ===

'''[[Glasgow-1376|James Glasgow]]''' is not a supported child of this family and should not be attached as a son born on 29 January 1657.

The cited record for that date is the baptism of Marion Glasgow and names James Glasgow as her father. It is not a birth or baptism record for a son named James.

=== Identity caution ===

This James should not be confused with '''[[Glasgow-3077|James Glasgow]]''', who married [[Clerk-460|Helen Clerk]] and was associated with [[Glasgow-3093|John Glasgow]].

The Edinburgh weaver is identified by:

* the 1641 apprenticeship naming him as a son of Robert Glasgow;
* his apprenticeship to William Sclaitter;
* his 1649 admission as an Edinburgh burgess;
* his occupation as a weaver;
* his marriages to Bessie Whyte and Agnes Duncan; and
* the 1686 burgess record identifying Marion Glasgow as his daughter.

=== Further research ===

Useful remaining records include:

* the original apprenticeship papers or incorporation records;
* records establishing whether [[Glasgow-1156|Robert Glasgow]] was the father named in the apprenticeship;
* records identifying James's mother;
* original baptism entries for each child;
* any further records establishing the children's mothers;
* a burial or testament for James;
* records identifying James's birthplace; and
* further records concerning William Calder and Marion Glasgow.

[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

{{Estimated Date}}

== Biography ==
'''William Glasgow''' was an adult member of the Larne and
Kilwaughter Presbyterian congregation by 1739/40.

The congregation's session accounts record William handling money
received from use of the mortcloth on 17 February 1739/40, in
October 1741 and on 29 December 1743.[https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184109/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/TheirStory2.html]

These entries cannot concern [[Glasgow-3326|William Glasgow]], born
in 1730, who was only about nine to thirteen years old. They establish
that a separate, older William Glasgow was present in the Larne
congregation.

William's date of birth is unknown. A compiled family reconstruction
associates him with a St Cedma's gravestone and gives a birth year of
about 1708. The same reconstruction elsewhere reports conflicting
tombstone-derived years of 1699 and 1708. No photograph or complete
transcription of the memorial has yet been inspected.

A probate index contains an entry for '''William Glasgow of Larne'''
in 1783. This record cannot presently be assigned securely to this
William because the younger William born in 1730 was also an adult
in the Larne area. The year 1783 should not therefore be treated as
This William's proved death year.

The compiled reconstruction implies that William had an eldest son
named '''James'''. It does not provide a baptism, date, mother's name,
will, deed or complete gravestone inscription identifying that son.
James may remain attached as an uncertain child and working hypothesis.
Given the estimated dates, a grandson or later descendant may be more
likely than a direct son; the attachment must not be presented as proved.

The reconstruction is internally inconsistent concerning a later
James Glasgow born about 1775. Its numbered family list places that
James on the same gravestone as the William born in 1730, rather than
This older William. The shared memorial does not itself establish a
father-and-son relationship.

No inspected contemporary record currently identifies William's wife.

William has been described as a son of [[Glasgow-1502|Robert Glasgow]]
and a brother of [[Glasgow-1504|James Glasgow]]. No inspected baptism,
will, deed, marriage settlement or gravestone transcription proves
either relationship. His description as an uncle of James's son
William is consequently also uncertain.


=== Larne leases and later proof of execution ===

A Registry of Deeds memorial records a lease dated 10 March 1736 from the Earl of Antrim to William Glasgow and [[Glasgow-1499|Hugh Glasgow]] of Larne for two tenements in Newtown of Larne. The lease names no relationship between William and Hugh. Its measuring lives were members of the royal family rather than members of the Glasgow family.<ref name="ROD1736">Registry of Deeds, memorial 63221, lease dated 10 March 1736, Earl of Antrim to William and Hugh Glasgow of Larne; registered 10 April 1738. Original image inspected 21 September 2026. [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSN1-FXR2 FamilySearch image].</ref>

A separate Earl of Antrim lease made in 1737 names William Glasgow of Larne as tenant of a house and garden in Old Town of Larne, on the north side of the street leading from Newtown toward the mill.<ref name="ROD1737">Registry of Deeds, memorial of Earl of Antrim lease to William Glasgow of Larne, made in 1737 and registered in 1739. [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-S3FM-8 FamilySearch image]. The automated transcript obscures part of the original date, so the image should be checked before publishing a verbatim transcription.</ref>

Most importantly, William Glasgow of Larne, described as a gentleman, witnessed a deed dated 19 April 1744 and personally proved its execution at Larne on 6 January 1775.<ref name="ROD1744">Registry of Deeds, memorial of deed dated 19 April 1744, with affidavit of William Glasgow at Larne on 6 January 1775. [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-C674 FamilySearch image].</ref> This directly carries an adult William of Larne from 1744 to 1775. It is much more consistent with this older William than with [[Glasgow-3326|William Glasgow]], reportedly born in 1730 and therefore only about fourteen in 1744. None of these deeds identifies William's parents, wife or children.

=== Joint lessors named in a 1757 assignment ===

A deed poll dated 4 June 1757, Matthew Stewart of Carncastle, farmer, to Robert Rainey of Larne, weaver, concerned a conditional assignment for £20 of Stewart's interest in a lease granted by [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]] and [[Glasgow-1499|Hugh Glasgow]] of Larne. The original memorial does not date their head lease or describe the holding sufficiently to identify it with the 1736 Newtown tenements.<ref name="JointLessors1757">Registry of Deeds, memorial 159181, manuscript pp. 473–474, deed dated 4 June 1757, registered 26 May 1761; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJM-MJX4 FamilySearch image 257, opening] and [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJM-MJP6 image 258, continuation], original images inspected 21 September 2026.</ref>

The joint names and Larne locality strongly support association with these lessees, but the record names no Glasgow relative or relationship between William and Hugh. Neither Glasgow executed this assignment; its registration in 1761 does not prove that either was then living. The separate 1751 and 1767 endorsements to the 1736 lease remain unexamined and may identify replacement lives.<ref>PRONI D2977/3A/4/81/72A, 1736 William and Hugh Glasgow lease with 1751 and 1767 endorsements; [https://apps.proni.gov.uk/eCatNI_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI eCatalogue], catalogue description only.</ref>

== Research Notes ==
The early session-account dates include:

* adult by 17 February 1739/40;
* living on 29 December 1743.

The dates about 1708 and 1783 should remain uncertain until the full
St Cedma's inscription or another direct record is examined.

The Larne and Kilwaughter Presbyterian collection at PRONI,
reference MIC/1B/6, includes baptisms from 1720 to 1769, marriages
from 1721 to 1769, session minutes and poor accounts. These records
should be searched for:

* a marriage of William Glasgow between approximately 1725 and 1740;
* baptisms of children of William Glasgow;
* a son James;
* any entry naming William's wife;
* references distinguishing the older William from William born
  in 1730.
  
== Possible Descendants ==

The precise identity of William's children has not been established from
an inspected baptism, will or deed. A plausible descendant reconstruction
can nevertheless be formed from Larne occupational, gravestone and family
naming evidence.

A possible son was '''James Glasgow''', a ropemaker who was already an
adult by 1760/61. An advertisement in the Belfast News-Letter of
2 January 1761 announced that “James Glasgow, Rope maker from Belfast”
had erected a ropewalk at Larne.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 2 January 1761,
advertisement by James Glasgow, ropemaker.</ref>

A compiled family chronology reports that James married '''Janet Shutter'''
in 1762 and had a son William about 1763.<ref>
[https://web.archive.org/web/20101124184247/http://lifesweaving.com/Glasgow/Kilwaughter/Timeline.html
Chronology of the Glasgow family in Northern Ireland].
</ref>

Alexander Holmes's will, dated 5 June 1799, refers to a field held with
James Glasgow and to houses occupied by “James Glasgow, Roper” in Old
Town, Larne.<ref>Registry of Deeds Abstracts of Wills, vol. III,
abstract of the will of Alexander Holmes of Larne, dated 5 June 1799;
RD 527/136/345729; PRONI T681, p.344.</ref>

No inspected record presently names the ropemaker's father. His age,
occupation and location make him a possible son of this William, but the
relationship remains uncertain.

The ropemaker's probable son was '''William Glasgow''', born about 1763
and died 5 October 1816. A published transcription of his gravestone in
Larne Parish Churchyard records his wife Elizabeth and daughters Jane
Shutter, Eliza and Mary.<ref>Francis Joseph Bigger and Herbert Hughes,
“Armorial Sculptured Stones of the County Antrim,” ''Ulster Journal of
Archaeology'', vol. VI (1900), p.47.</ref>

The inscription records:

* Jane Shutter Glasgow, died 21 April 1799 aged nine months;
* William Glasgow, died 5 October 1816 aged 53;
* his wife Elizabeth, died 17 September 1832 aged 60;
* their daughter Eliza, died 25 April 1839 aged 37; and
* their daughter Mary, died 18 October 1844 aged 37.

The name '''Jane Shutter Glasgow''' provides significant evidence that
William was connected with James Glasgow and Janet Shutter. The compiled
chronology identifies William's wife as Elizabeth Stewart of Corran and
records a daughter Elizabeth on 30 August 1802. This daughter may have
been the Eliza named on the gravestone.

James Glasgow, born about 1773/75 and currently attached as William's
uncertain son, may instead have belonged to this later generation. If
The ropemaker James was William's son, James born about 1773/75 would
probably have been William's grandson. The existing uncertain attachment
is retained as a working hypothesis pending identification of the
reported shared gravestone or another family record.

The chronology's identification of the ropemaker as a son of Hugh Glasgow
appears problematic. A published transcription of Hugh's family stone
records his son James as dying on 14 April 1812 aged 64, implying birth
about 1748. He would have been too young to establish the ropewalk in
1761 or marry in 1762. The chronology may therefore have combined two
different men named James Glasgow.

== Research Notes: Parentage and Larne Associations ==

William's parentage has not been proved. The present attachment to Robert
Glasgow is derived from the existing family tree; no inspected baptism, will,
deed or congregational minute names Robert as William's father.

A published transcript of the Larne and Kilwaughter congregational accounts
records that in 1734 the congregation's mortcloth or funeral pall was lodged
with “William Glasgow Major”. Accounts relating to the pall continued until
1759. This is a plausible early occurrence of the present William, although
The entry names no relatives and does not by itself establish identity.<ref>
Classon Porter, “Congregational Memoirs—Larne and Kilwaughter,”
''The Christian Unitarian'', vol. 3 (1864), p. 230.</ref>

Registry of Deeds memorial 62131, concerning a deed dated 10 March 1736,
describes William Glasgow as an adjoining occupier at Larne.<ref>Registry of
Deeds, memorial 62131, vol. 84, p. 481, deed dated 10 March 1736.</ref>

A separate Earl of Antrim lease from March 1736 leased New Town of Larne
tenements jointly to William Glasgow and Hugh Glasgow, both of Larne.<ref>
Registry of Deeds, memorial 63221; PRONI D300/2/1/100/3A-B.</ref> Related
lease endorsements survive under PRONI D2977/3A/4/81/72A. The joint tenancy
proves a close property association but does not state that William and Hugh
were brothers.

The surviving congregational extracts for 1699–1700 distinguish John Glasgow
senior of Kilwaughter, Robert Glasgow of the South Side and James Glasgow,
who was appointed overseer for Kilwaughter. No family relationship between
these men is stated.<ref>Classon Porter, “Congregational Memoirs—Larne and
Kilwaughter,” ''The Christian Unitarian'', vols. 2–3 (1863–1864),
transcript of the congregational records for 1699–1700.</ref>

The Connor diocesan probate index records William Glasgow of Larne in 1783. This is a possible match, not a secure identification: more than one adult William Glasgow was associated with Larne. PRONI reports that the original documents do not survive; the index supplies no relatives or exact death date. The estate year must not be treated as this William's proved death year.<ref>[https://apps.proni.gov.uk/ProniNames_IE/SearchPage.aspx PRONI Name Search], Connor diocesan probate index, William Glasgow, Larne, 1783.</ref>

Hugh, James, William and the younger Robert Glasgow should therefore be
treated as members of an East Antrim research cluster rather than proved
siblings unless a direct relationship record is found.

=== Unidentified William Glasgow, deed witness in 1772 ===
A lease dated 12 May 1772 from John Miller, currier of Gardenmore in Old Town of Larne, to David Drennan, weaver, names Wm Glasgow, David Dickey and James Fairies, all of Larne, as witnesses. Either [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]] or [[Glasgow-3326|William Glasgow]] could be this witness; the deed gives no age, occupation or relative to distinguish them. The son William named in the trust clause is Drennan's son, not a Glasgow relationship. Registration on 9 November 1784 does not prove that the witness William Glasgow was still alive then.<ref>Registry of Deeds, Miller to Drennan, lease 12 May 1772, registered 9 November 1784, manuscript p. 315, image 166; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-SQLT-3 original image], inspected 21 September 2026.</ref>

== Biography ==
'''James Glasgow''' was reportedly born in '''1737'''. A Larne or Kilwaughter congregational record is said to contain an entry for a James, son of [[Glasgow-1499|Hugh Glasgow]], at '''New Town, Larne''', in that year.

The original congregational entry, or a reliable full transcription, has not yet been cited on this profile. The exact birth date, place and identification of Hugh as James’s father should therefore be treated as probable rather than conclusively established.

James was a '''ropemaker''' at Larne, County Antrim. A lease dated 10 September 1760, registered on 24 November 1763, describes him as a ropemaker of Belfast and leases him a marked-out ropewalk at Gardenmore in Larne for thirty-one years from 1 November 1760. He agreed to build a house at the south end of the ropewalk.<ref name="Ropewalk1760">Registry of Deeds transcript, lease dated 10 September 1760 and registered 24 November 1763, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-S7XZ-8 FamilySearch image].</ref>

On 28 March 1768 James, described as a ropemaker of the Old Town of Larne, assigned the plot, workhouse and remainder of the same lease to John Hill for £50. The matching commencement date and rent identify it as the 1760 ropewalk.<ref name="Ropewalk1768">Registry of Deeds transcript, assignment dated 28 March 1768, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJW-DDXW FamilySearch image].</ref>


A memorial at '''St Cedma’s Church, Larne''', is reported to record James Glasgow with the dates '''1737–1802''' and to name his wife as '''Janet Shutter'''. A photograph or complete reliable transcription of the monument should be cited before the exact dates and marriage are treated as fully verified.

James is reported to have died in '''1802'''.

An Irish probate-index transcription records a '''James Glasgow of Larne''' in the Diocese of Belfast in '''1803'''.<ref>Irish probate index transcription supplied July 2026, entry for James Glasgow, Diocese of Belfast, residence Larne, 1803.</ref>

The agreement in name and residence, together with probate in the year after the reported death, makes this a strong match to the man commemorated at St Cedma’s.

The 1803 entry should be understood as a probate or estate event. It does not replace the reported 1802 death year. Probate occurring in the year following death would be ordinary.

The probate entry establishes Larne as James’s recorded residence during the estate proceedings. It does not by itself prove that Larne was his place of death.

=== Wife and family ===

James’s wife is reported on the St Cedma’s memorial as '''Janet Shutter'''.

The complete inscription should be obtained and cited because the memorial may also contain:

* Janet’s dates;
* the date or duration of the marriage;
* children buried in the same plot;
* other Glasgow relatives; or
* wording clarifying whether the monument was erected by descendants.

No inspected baptismal, marriage, will or probate record currently cited on this profile names James’s children.

The 1803 probate record may be important. An original will, administration bond or surviving abstract could identify:

* Janet as his widow;
* sons or daughters;
* married daughters or sons-in-law;
* executors or administrators;
* business partners;
* property at Larne or Blackcave; or
* other relatives.

== Research Notes ==
=== Identification and evidence ===

The following records probably concern the same man:

* the James, son of Hugh Glasgow, reportedly recorded at New Town or Larne in 1737;
* James Glasgow, ropemaker, documented in the 1760 ropewalk lease and 1768 assignment;
* James Glasgow commemorated at St Cedma’s with dates 1737–1802 and wife Janet Shutter; and
* James Glasgow of Larne whose estate entered Belfast probate in 1803.

The chronology and repeated Larne association make this identification plausible and probably correct.

The strongest direct contemporary evidence presently cited is the 1760 ropewalk lease and its 1768 assignment. The baptism and memorial evidence still require complete source citations, and the probate index does not name James’s father or wife.

The profile should therefore distinguish between:

* directly documented facts, including James’s ropemaking and Larne residence in the 1760–1773 records;
* strong identity matches, including the 1803 probate entry; and
* reported but not yet fully exposed evidence, including the 1737 congregational entry and St Cedma’s memorial.

=== Ropemaker evidence and identity distinction ===

A Registry of Deeds memorial dated 14 May 1766 also names James Glasgow, ropemaker of Larne, as a witness.<ref>[https://www.irishdeedsindex.net/mem.php?memorial=204122 Registry of Deeds Index Project, memorial 204122], deed dated 14 May 1766.</ref> In 1773 Mr James Glasgow of Larne, gentleman, swore that he was aged upwards of thirty, placing his birth before 27 October 1743.<ref name="Larne1773">Registry of Deeds memorial and affidavit, sworn 27 October 1773, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSH3-M72W-M FamilySearch image].</ref> Alexander Holmes's 1799 will later identifies a Larne occupant as James Glasgow, roper. The repeated occupation and place form a coherent sequence.

The 1768 assignment was witnessed by a '''different''' James Glasgow who was expressly described as a tanner. A 1778 mortgage and the 1786 Blackcave lease continue that tanner sequence and fit [[Glasgow-3991|James Glasgow (about 1747–1812)]]. The two tradesmen should not be conflated.

The reported 1737 congregational occurrence and the present uncertain placement under [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]] remain competing parentage hypotheses until the original entry or another relationship record is inspected.

=== Research priorities ===

Further research should obtain:

* the original or fullest available congregational entry for the 1737 James, son of Hugh Glasgow;
* the name of the congregation and exact wording of that entry;
* a photograph or complete transcription of the St Cedma’s memorial;
* evidence supporting Janet Shutter’s identity and marriage to James;
* the exact nature of the 1803 Belfast probate entry;
* the original will, administration record or bond, if it survives;
* a Betham or other pre-destruction abstract of the estate;
* names of beneficiaries, executors, witnesses or sureties; and
* records identifying any children of James and Janet.

=== Research conclusion ===

James Glasgow was directly recorded as a ropemaker in the 1760 Larne ropewalk lease, the 1766 memorial and the 1768 assignment.

The 1803 Belfast probate entry for James Glasgow of Larne is a strong match to the man reportedly commemorated at St Cedma’s with dates 1737–1802. It supports Larne as his probate residence while remaining consistent with death in 1802.

The reported identification of his wife as Janet Shutter and his father as Hugh Glasgow is plausible, but the complete memorial and congregational record should be cited before those relationships and the exact dates are treated as certain.

=== Current Larne reconstruction ===

James is securely the Belfast/Larne ropemaker in the 1760 Gardenmore ropewalk lease and its 1768 assignment, and the 1773 affidavit places that adult James at Larne and over thirty. The 1768 document separately calls its witness James Glasgow a tanner; that is a different occupational record group, probably [[Glasgow-3991|James Glasgow]], and does not change this James's occupation. The original 1784 lease registered in 1790 has now been inspected: its witness is explicitly a tanner and belongs to the separate occupational sequence probably represented by [[Glasgow-3991|James Glasgow]]. James is a plausible earlier-generation candidate in the Larne reconstruction, including as a possible father of [[Glasgow-3902|Adam Glasgow]] and possible kin of [[Glasgow-3904|older Alexander Glasgow]], but no record yet makes either relationship. His 1762 marriage to Janet Shutter postdates Adam's estimated 1758 birth, so Janet cannot be called Adam's mother. A William Glasgow, merchant, witnessed the 1760 lease, but is not yet definitely [[Glasgow-1505|William Glasgow]].<ref name="LarneCurrent">Registry of Deeds memorials for the 1760 lease, 1768 assignment and 1773 affidavit, cited above.</ref>

=== Additional source context ===

These contextual and comparison sources supplement the individual record assessments above; they do not supply a missing parental statement.
* Related profile: [[Glasgow-1509]].
<ref name="Retained2">[https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJ4-4SJF Registry of Deeds, 1784 transaction registered in 1790: James Glasgow, tanner; sworn 17 August and registered 23 August 1790].</ref>


A lease dated 14 January 1784 was witnessed by James Glasgow of Larne, '''tanner''', with Samuel Drummond, merchant, and James Farries, writing clerk. James’s affidavit was sworn 17 August 1790; the memorial was registered on 23 August. The original reads “Tanner”, resolving an earlier automated “Turner” reading. This strengthens the occupational sequence, without independently naming his family.<ref name="Tanner1784">Registry of Deeds, memorial 278037, lease 14 January 1784, sworn 17 August and registered 23 August 1790, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CSJ4-4SJF FamilySearch image 437], original inspected 21 September 2026. The online collection label 1734–1736 does not describe this image’s date.</ref>

=== Newtown title succession: identities unresolved ===

An 1874 deed recites a lease to James Glasgow dated 2 October 1779 and its renewal to Anne Glasgow and Jane Glasgow on 25 February 1832. The north-side Newtown property, formerly John English’s, adjoined a tenement formerly Hugh Glasgow’s. This documents succession to a lease, but does not call the women James’s daughters or identify which James held it. The monument wife Jane of [[Glasgow-3991|James Glasgow]] died in 1820 and cannot automatically be the 1832 Jane. [[Glasgow-3992|Ann Glasgow]], whose monument gives a May 1832 death, is only a candidate for Anne; the original renewal is needed.<ref name="Newtown1874">Registry of Deeds, Antrim to John Mulvenna, indenture 25 March 1874, registered 24 August 1874, [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CS54-77Q4-H FamilySearch image 475], recital inspected in the original; [https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3Q9M-CS54-77QC-T continuation image 476].</ref>

Glasgow-3322.remote_wikitext:
{{One Name Study|name=Glasgow}}

== Biography ==

'''Daniel Glasco''' was associated with Lower Norfolk County in the Colony of Virginia during the late seventeenth century. His date and place of birth have not been identified.

The spelling '''Glasco''' is used in the published abstract of the only contemporary record presently identified for him. The original record should be inspected before concluding that this was his consistent surname spelling.

May be a grandson of [[Glasgow-1157|Robert Glasgow II (abt.1612-abt.1690)]]

=== Marriage to Mary Gamon ===

Daniel married '''Mary Gamon''', also rendered Gammon in later accounts, before 4 October 1693.

The will of Mary's father, '''John Gamon''', was dated 4 October 1693 and proved on 15 March 1694. Its published abstract identifies Daniel Glasco as John Gamon's son-in-law and Mary as Daniel's wife. John left Daniel and Mary eighty acres of land bordering Richford Swamp.<ref name="GamonWill">Charles Fleming McIntosh, ''Brief Abstract of Lower Norfolk County and Norfolk County Wills, 1637–1710'' (Virginia: Colonial Dames of America in the State of Virginia, 1914), p. 149, abstract of the will of John Gamon, dated 4 October 1693 and proved 15 March 1694; cited and discussed in Legacy Tree Genealogists, [https://www.legacytree.com/wp-content/uploads/T1508095.CLIENTGlasgow1508.report.public.pdf ''Research Report''] (1 March 2016), p. 3.</ref>

The record directly establishes that:

* Daniel and Mary were married by 4 October 1693;
* Mary's father was John Gamon; and
* Daniel and Mary received land bordering Richford Swamp.

Richford Swamp was situated in Elizabeth River Parish, Lower Norfolk County.<ref name="LegacyReport">Legacy Tree Genealogists, [https://www.legacytree.com/wp-content/uploads/T1508095.CLIENTGlasgow1508.report.public.pdf ''Research Report''] (1 March 2016), pp. 3–4.</ref>

The will abstract does not identify Daniel's parents, birthplace, age, occupation or children.

Daniel was alive on 4 October 1693. His date and place of death have not been identified.

== Research Notes ==

=== Birth date ===

Daniel has previously been assigned a birth year of 1613.

The cited source for that date is an International Genealogical Index entry submitted by an unidentified contributor. The entry contains no supporting source information.<ref name="IGI">The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, “International Genealogical Index (IGI),” database, ''FamilySearch'', [https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/2:1:MDL3-HTF entry for Daniel Glasgow] (accessed 4 April 2025); submitted by user jence5408, with no source information supplied.</ref>

A submitted IGI entry records a contributor's assertion. Without an underlying baptism, Bible, will, deed or other historical record, it does not establish that Daniel was born in 1613.

Daniel's birth date and birthplace should therefore be left unknown.

For database purposes, the only certain statement is that he was born before 4 October 1693, when he was recorded as Mary's husband.

=== Unsupported Scottish parentage ===

'''[[Glasgow-1156|Robert Glasgow]]''' and '''[[Ivey-2264|Deborah Ivey]]''' have previously been attached as Daniel's parents.

No inspected record identifies either person as his father or mother.

The will of John Gamon identifies Daniel's wife and father-in-law but does not name Daniel's parents. No Scottish baptism, marriage, testament, land record or migration record has been found connecting Daniel with Robert Glasgow or Deborah Ivey.

Both parental relationships should be removed.

Daniel should also not be attached as a child of '''[[Glasgow-3938|Robert Glasgow]]''', the cordiner who married Jonet or Janet Thomsone in Edinburgh in 1652. No evidence connects that Edinburgh household with Daniel or colonial Virginia.

=== Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson tradition ===

Many online family trees instead identify Daniel as a son of a Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson or Johnston.

A professional review of the family found that this relationship was repeated in online trees but that those trees supplied no documentary evidence supporting it.<ref name="LegacyReport" />

No contemporary record presently establishes that:

* Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson were Daniel's parents;
* Daniel was born in Scotland;
* Daniel migrated from Scotland to Virginia; or
* Daniel belonged to the Scottish Glasgow families represented by the earlier profiles.

Any attachment to Robert Glasgow and Ann Johnson should remain uncertain or be removed until a contemporary parentage record is found.

=== Possible connection with Robert Glascocke ===

A Robert Glascocke was documented in the Elizabeth River area before Daniel's known appearance there.

Robert Glascocke received:

* a patent for 200 acres in Elizabeth City County on 7 October 1635; and
* a patent for another fifty acres in Lower New Norfolk County on 10 June 1639.

A 1640 court order also referred to religious services being held at Robert Glascocke's house while a meetinghouse was being built.<ref name="LegacyReport" />

The shared locality and broadly similar surnames make Robert Glascocke a person worth investigating as a possible relative.

They do not prove that:

* Robert Glascocke was Daniel's father;
* Glascocke and Glasco were forms used by the same family;
* Robert married Ann Johnson;
* Daniel inherited Robert's land; or
* either man belonged to a Scottish Glasgow family.

Robert Glascocke should not be attached as Daniel's father without a deed, will, court record or other document connecting them.

=== Surname ===

The published abstract of John Gamon's will records Daniel's surname as '''Glasco'''.

Later records and compiled genealogies use variants including:

* Glasco;
* Glasgow;
* Glascock;
* Glasscock; and
* Glascocke.

Surname spelling was not fully standardised during this period, but similarity alone does not prove that all these records concern one family.

The original will should be inspected to establish the spelling used by the clerk. Until then, Glasco is the best-supported spelling for Daniel himself, with Glasgow retained as an alternate form where appropriate.

=== Children ===

No inspected contemporary record identifies a child of Daniel Glasco and Mary Gamon.

Later family trees attribute children and extensive descendants to the couple, but those relationships should not be treated as established solely because they appear in compiled genealogies.

Each proposed child requires separate evidence, such as:

* a baptism or parish entry;
* a deed describing the relationship;
* a will naming the child;
* a guardianship record;
* an apprenticeship record;
* a court order; or
* a documented chain of inherited land.

Any existing child attachments should remain uncertain pending review of their individual evidence.

=== The inherited property ===

John Gamon's will left Daniel and Mary eighty acres bordering Richford Swamp.

Tracing that property may be the best route for identifying Daniel's later life and possible children. Deeds involving its later sale, inheritance or division may name Daniel's heirs or establish whether he had died.

The original will, probate proceedings and subsequent land records should be obtained rather than relying solely on the published abstract.

=== Death ===

Daniel's date and place of death are unknown.

He was alive when John Gamon's will was written on 4 October 1693. The will's probate on 15 March 1694 does not necessarily prove Daniel was still living on that later date.

His death should therefore be recorded as after 4 October 1693 only if an estimated date is required. No precise death place should be assigned.

=== Further research ===

Useful remaining records include:

* the original will of John Gamon;
* the complete probate file and estate accounts;
* deeds concerning the eighty acres bordering Richford Swamp;
* Lower Norfolk County court orders;
* Elizabeth River Parish records;
* later Norfolk and Princess Anne County deeds and probate records;
* records identifying Daniel and Mary's children or heirs;
* land records concerning Robert Glascocke's patents;
* evidence establishing whether Glasco, Glasgow and Glascocke were used for the same family;
* contemporary records concerning Ann Johnson or Johnston;
* any immigration or transportation record for Daniel;
* a will or estate administration for Daniel;
* a will or estate administration for Mary; and
* the original evidence underlying the submitted IGI entry.

== Sources ==

== Acknowledgements ==

This profile was previously attached to an unsupported Scottish family and carried an unsourced birth year of 1613. It has been revised to represent Daniel Glasco, husband of Mary Gamon, documented through the 1693–1694 will of John Gamon.

Glasgow-3373.public_addition_wikitext:
A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Adam D. Glasgow of Broughshane appears in the Royal Belfast Academical Institution school prizes in June 1830 and Belfast College examinations reported in May 1831. The 1831 report also names James Glasgow, Institution, in voluntary advanced mathematical examinations.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 29 June 1830, p.3, Royal Belfast Academical Institution School Department; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390569859/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 6 May 1831, p.3, Belfast College report dated 30 April; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390545285/ record].</ref> [[Glasgow-1781|Adam Dickie Glasgow]] and James McClure [[Glasgow-1780]] are strong compatible candidates. The newspaper gives no ages or parents and does not call these men brothers. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Adam D. Glasgow resigned as an assistant in the Royal Belfast Institution’s Mathematical and Mercantile School in December 1836. Rev. Adam D. Glasgow received a unanimous call to Berry Street Presbyterian Church, Belfast, in January 1840 and was its newly ordained minister at a congregational presentation on 5 March.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 10 January 1837, p.2, resignation presentation on 22 December 1836; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390542489/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 17 January 1840, p.2, Berry Street ministerial call; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390553900/ record]; Belfast News-Letter, 10 March 1840, p.2, Berry Street soiree on 5 March; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390555182/ record].</ref> The repeated name and institutional setting support the education/teaching continuity; the ministerial continuation and attribution to [[Glasgow-1781|Adam Dickie Glasgow]] remain qualified. The newspaper does not spell out Dickie or identify parents. 5 March is the presentation date, not a proved ordination date. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. A marriage notice reports that on 30 December 1841 Rev. Adam Glasgow married Miss Jane Thompson at the house of her uncle, Thomas Corbett, Esq., on May-street. The date 30 December is derived from “30th ult.” in the 4 January issue.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 4 January 1842, p. 3, marriage notice for Rev. Adam Glasgow and Miss Jane Thompson; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390552100/ record].</ref> The notice records Rev. Adam Glasgow as groom and Miss Jane Thompson as bride, married on 30 December 1841 (derived from “30th ult.” in the 4 January 1842 issue). Thomas Corbett is described as the bride’s uncle; no parentage or family branch is stated. May-street identifies the house where the notice says the wedding took place, not Adam’s residence. This is compatible with, but does not prove, identification of the bride as the tree-linked Jane Fulton (Thompson) Glasgow or the groom as [[Glasgow-1781]]. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. A designation report names the Rev. Adam Glasgow among four ministers set apart as missionaries to India and explicitly says he was “brother of the Rev. Jas. Glasgow.”<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 14 January 1842, p. 2, designation of four missionaries to India; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390552341/ record].</ref> The report explicitly describes the named Rev. Adam Glasgow as brother of Rev. Jas. Glasgow. This is a report of the same missionary-designation service also reported by the Freeman’s Journal on 14 January 1842; independence between reports is not assumed. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. An India Mission prayer-meeting notice reports that letters from Rev. Adam Glasgow and Rev. Mr. Spier were read at Rosemary-street Church.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 28 March 1843, p. 2, India Mission prayer meeting and letters; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560193/ record].</ref> The notice names Rev. Adam Glasgow as a letter author in the India Mission context. It gives no middle name, home locality, or unique identity bridge. The Belfast church is the meeting venue, not a stated residence or congregation for Adam. This is consistent with, but does not uniquely identify, [[Glasgow-1781]]. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. A report of the 10 March 1841 meeting at Rev. Dr. Hanna’s Rosemary-street Church names Rev. Adam Glasgow among the clergy “on and around the platform.” Malone follows Rev. Joseph M’Kenzie, not Adam.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 12 March 1841, p. 3, clergy and deputation meeting/platform report; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390556571/ record].</ref> This report identifies Rev. Adam Glasgow among clergy at the meeting; it does not state his residence or uniquely identify him as [[Glasgow-1781]]. Malone belongs to Rev. Joseph M’Kenzie. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. At the Townsend-street congregational and Sabbath-School soiree on 18 August 1840, devotional exercises were conducted by “the Rev. Adam Glasgow, of Berry-street.” “Of Berry-street” is his printed church association, not proof of residence.<ref>Belfast News-Letter, 21 August 1840, p. 2, Townsend-street congregational and Sabbath-School soiree; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/390560975/ record].</ref> “Of Berry-street” is the printed church association for Rev. Adam Glasgow, not proof of residence. A separate later passage names Rev. James Glasgow, Missionary to India; this is compatible with [[Glasgow-1780]] but does not uniquely identify him. Their co-occurrence is not evidence of kinship. The identification remains uncertain.

A possible identification concerns Adam D. Glasgow, Broughshane student and Belfast teacher/minister. Marriage notice: on 25 July 1840 (reported as “25th ult.”), Mr James Small, of Lottery Cottage, county Armagh, married Miss Margaret Small of this town; the officiant was Rev. Glasgow-4100.public_addition_wikitext:
A possible identification concerns James Glasgow, master of the Prosperity of Irvine. James Glasgow is named in the Greenock arrival list headed “Greenock, August 12”: “The Prosperity of Irvine, James Glasgow, from Northcopen.” The item was published in The Caledonian Mercury on 18 August 1740, page 3.<ref>The Caledonian Mercury, 18 August 1740, page 3, Greenock shipping list; [https://www.newspapers.com/image/394559372/ record].</ref> The ship–homeport–master–origin format supports reading James as the shipmaster. No age, relatives or personal residence are stated. Irvine is the ship’s homeport and Greenock the reporting locality; neither proves James’s birthplace. Northcopen is retained without an unverified modern-place identification. The identification remains uncertain.

=== Possible Irvine birth family ===

Select John [[Glasgow-2475]] of the Irvine Isabell Kyle/Kelle household as the possible working father of James [[Glasgow-4157]], Helen Nasmith’s partner, at 58% subjective confidence. The leading explanation identifies the later James with John and Isabell’s James, baptised at Irvine on 19 August 1711 ([[Glasgow-4100]]). This joins a specific recorded birth family to a specific later household in the same parish. Assuming infant baptism, that James would be about thirty when John was born in August 1741 and about thirty-five at Susanna’s 1747 birth. The later household’s first known son is John, agreeing with the proposed paternal grandfather. Same-parish continuity, a comfortable adult chronology and this modest naming clue together favour this family over the younger 1721 comparison. None independently proves the identification.

The 58% assesses the complete father proposition, including the uncertain baptism-to-adult identity. No source names the 1741–1747 father’s own parents, and no residence, trade or witness links the households. Baptism is not necessarily near birth, John is a common forename, and the first known child is not necessarily the eldest child. The 1711 and 1721 ages are illustrative infant-baptism assumptions, not recorded ages. James [[Glasgow-4157]]’s before-1722 birth is an inherited adult-age estimate, not a 1722 birth or a hard biological boundary. Do not use that estimate to prefer or exclude a candidate. All dates and identities remain unchanged. The original registers are uninspected; maintained Findmypast transcripts are being reassessed, not newly discovered.

Retain James [[Glasgow-4158]] as an unselected alternative father at 26%, through possible identification of Helen Nasmith’s partner with his son James [[Glasgow-4129]], baptised at Irvine on 11 April 1721 to James and Margaret Rae. If baptised as an infant, he would be about twenty at the 1741 child’s birth: young but fully possible, not excluded. The Rae household and its Margaret/Marion distinction remain as previously assessed. James [[Glasgow-1932]], baptised at Kilwinning in 1707 to John Glasgow and Mary Gemill, and James [[Glasgow-1131]], indexed at Kilbirnie in 1718 to John Glasgow and Agnes Ferguson, remain broader compatible comparisons; their father’s name could also explain a John child, so naming is not unique. An unrepresented family is also possible. No new individual percentages are assigned to these unselected broader identity comparisons. Another compatible model identifies Helen Nasmith’s partner with the older Rae-household James [[Glasgow-4158]] himself, after a different partnership. His inherited age estimate would make him at least about thirty-nine in 1741, which does not exclude this model. No spouse death or remarriage is established. This is distinct from the 26% model making the later man a son of James [[Glasgow-4158]]; neither identity is merged. Hugh [[Glasgow-3109]]’s existing uncertain attachment belongs to the elder account and is not transferred to James [[Glasgow-4157]].

This is one newly selected possible father, not a confident relationship or a source discovery. The Irvine James, John, Allan and Susanna household provisionally joins the larger working component; supported and confident connectivity do not gain this 58% edge. James’s documented fatherhood of the three children remains separately 98%. His identification with the Prosperity shipmaster in 1740 remains unresolved and supplies no family bridge. John [[Glasgow-2475]]’s own uncertain upstream pedigree is not strengthened. Isabell Kyle is not selected as James [[Glasgow-4157]]’s mother. [[Glasgow-4100]] and [[Glasgow-4157]] may be two accounts of one person: no merge is performed and the working profile count is not a count of distinct proved people or two independently established James brothers. Resolve the possible duplicate before any live attachment or merger.

Compare the original Irvine 1711 and 1721 baptism entries with the 1741, 1743 and 1747 entries for occupations, addresses and witnesses; seek a James–Helen marriage or earlier child. Those details could distinguish the birth identities without relying on naming. Reassess the 58% and 26% together when a discriminating record appears.<ref name="IrvineUpstream2026">[https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F3572963&tab=this Findmypast, Irvine OPR595/1 p.16, James Glasgow baptism, 19 August 1711; parents John Glasgow and Isabell Kelle; SCOT/OPR/BAP/3572963, maintained transcript]; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F3573667&tab=this Findmypast, Irvine OPR595/1 p.29, James Glasgow baptism, 11 April 1721; parents James Glasgow and Margt Rae; SCOT/OPR/BAP/3573667, maintained transcript]; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F3575071&tab=this Findmypast, Irvine OPR595/1, John Glasgow baptism, 1741; maintained 3 September 2026 transcript, SCOT/OPR/BAP/3575071]; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F3575202&tab=this Findmypast, Irvine OPR595/1, Allan Glasgow baptism, 1743; maintained 3 September 2026 transcript, SCOT/OPR/BAP/3575202]; [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F3575478&tab=this Findmypast, Irvine OPR595/1, Susanna Glasgow baptism, 1747; maintained 3 September 2026 transcript, SCOT/OPR/BAP/3575478].</ref>

== Biography ==

'''James Glasgow''' was baptised at Irvine, Ayrshire, on 11 Apr 1721. The parish register names his father as [[Glasgow-4158|James Glasgow]] and his mother as [[Rae-3513|Margaret Rae]].<ref name="FMP1" /> Because the entry records a baptism rather than a birth, his birth is placed before that date, and Irvine is inferred from the baptism rather than independently recorded.

== Research Notes ==

The baptism is the only record found for James Glasgow. A search of live WikiTree profiles found no compatible match; [[Glasgow-1024|James]], [[Glasgow-1442|James]], [[Glasgow-2868|James]], [[Glasgow-2916|James]], [[Glasgow-2988|James]], [[Glasgow-3523|James]] belongs to a different family and is not this person.

== Biography ==

'''James Glasgow''' lived at Irvine, Ayrshire, where the parish register names him as the father of three children baptised between 1741 and 1747. Their mother was [[Nasmith-38|Helen Nasmith]], named in the same entries:

* [[Glasgow-4116|John Glasgow]], baptised 6 August 1741
* [[Glasgow-4110|Allan Glasgow]], baptised 22 May 1743
* [[Glasgow-4128|Susanna Glasgow]], baptised 29 March 1747

No birth or baptism record for James himself has been found, so his birth is placed before 1722, the year by which he must have been born to father John in 1741. Irvine is inferred from his children's baptisms and is not independently recorded.<ref name="IrvineOPR">Findmypast, ''Scotland, Parish Births & Baptisms 1564–1929'', Irvine, Ayrshire, Old Parish Register OPR 595/1; the individual baptism entries are cited on each child's profile, for example [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F3575071&tab=this John Glasgow, 1741].</ref>

== Research Notes ==

James and Helen are linked only by the recurring father and mother names in the Irvine register. No record of James's own parents, birth or death has been found.

== Biography ==

James Glasgow is named as a father in two Irvine, Ayrshire, baptism entries. [[Glasgow-4129|James Glasgow]] was baptised on 11 April 1721 with parents James Glasgow and [[Rae-3513|Margaret Rae]]. [[Glasgow-4120|William Glasgow]] was baptised on 3 February 1723 with parents James Glasgow and [[Rae-3515|Marion Rae]].<ref name="James1721">Findmypast, ''Scotland, Parish Births & Baptisms 1564–1929'', Irvine Old Parish Register, [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F3573667&tab=this James Glasgow baptism, 11 April 1721]. The individual child profile gives the full indexed entry.</ref><ref name="William1723">Findmypast, ''Scotland, Parish Births & Baptisms 1564–1929'', Irvine Old Parish Register, [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FOPR%2FBAP%2F3573825&tab=this William Glasgow baptism, 3 February 1723]. The individual child profile gives the full indexed entry.</ref>

No birth, baptism or death record has been identified for this adult James. His birth before about 1702 is an adult-age estimate from the 1721 child; Irvine is his recorded household locality, not a proved birthplace.

== Research Notes ==

The former father profile Glasgow-4164, based on the 1723 William entry, was merged into this profile on 27 September 2026. The same uncommon father name and Rae surname in the same Irvine parish within two years, with no separate identified James, support one adult identity. The maternal given names differ: Margaret and Marion may refer to distinct women or to a transcription/register variation. Both named mothers and both baptism entries are preserved; no marriage, death or remarriage between 1721 and 1723 is asserted without a record.

The birth estimates on the two former profiles were derived only from the children's dates. Compare the original 1721 and 1723 register pages and search Irvine marriage or burial entries for the two Rae names.

Glasgow-1549.remote_wikitext: == Biography == John Glasgow was the progenitor of the Glasgow family in Blair, Cambria, Clearfield and Huntingdon Counties of Central Pennsylvania. John Glasgow (who is being designated as John Glasgow the 1st) and his wife Margaret Hunter were prominent citizens of Glasgow, Scotland. They and their two young sons Richard and John(2) sailed for America in 1781. The exact year when John Glasgow and his wife came to America was established when Margaret had a son, William, on the voyage over. In the Census records the place of birth for William Glasgow is shown as the Ocean, or the Atlantic Ocean and the year of birth as 1781. It is not known what ship they sailed or specifically what the reason was for their leaving their homeland. One account has them sailing from Ireland and landing in Delaware. This could be accurate as in the late 1600s, England had sent groups of Scotch to Ireland to defend the various interests of England. The Scotch established themselves in Ireland, then England deliberately crushed Irish commerce and industries by enacting laws prohibiting the export of cattle, milk, butter, cheese, and later woolens. The English treatment of Ireland had tow results as far as immigration: (1) the economy of Ireland gradually declined which resulted in lower standard of living and (2) among the Scotch-Irish, dislike of the English grew. THe American Revolution received much sympathy in the Presbyterians who were prohibited from holding office. Most Scots were Presbyterians. Consider the economic climate in Ireland compared to what the Scotch in Ireland perceived the climate to be in America. In the New Country there was untold quantities of land available, just for moving onto it and improving it; wild game in large quantities, with no prohibition on shooting it; timber and firewood is unlimited amounts (lumber was scarce in Ireland). It is not wonder that the people immigrated to America where life certainly was difficult and harsh but no more so than they had been used to in Ireland; and they had much more control of their destiny here. It is hard for us to imagine what life was like for the early immigrants as they arrived and settled in this area. We have no detailed record of the Glasgows early experiences in this country. == Sources == * https://www.familysearch.org/tree/person/details/G7MK-866 * Will of John Glasgow. "Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994," images, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/3:1:3QS7-L99B-T8NH?cc=1999196&wc=9PM6-7MN%3A268496101%2C268530601 : 3 July 2014), Huntingdon > Wills 1822-1847 vol 3-4 > image 103 of 607; county courthouses, Pennsylvania.

'''James Glasgow''' was probably born about 1680. This is an uncertain estimate from his 1696 apprenticeship; his age and birthplace were not recorded. Edinburgh is usable only as an uncertain location inferred from the apprenticeship and his father's burgess status.

On 22 April 1696 James, son of James Glasgow, weaver and burgess, was entered as apprentice to William Adam, apothecary and burgess of Edinburgh.<ref name="Apprentice1696">Henry Paton, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/edinburgh_apprentices_~_1666_to_1700_~_1929.pdf ''Register of Apprentices of the City of Edinburgh, 1666–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1929), printed p. 37, entry dated 22 April 1696; see also Findmypast, [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FEDINBURGH%2FAPPRENTICES%2F0005161%2F1&tab=this transcript SCOT/EDINBURGH/APPRENTICES/0005161/1], captured 3 September 2026.</ref>

== Research Notes ==

The Findmypast transcript renders the master as William Adamson. The published register reads “Wm. Adam”; that reading is used here.

[[Glasgow-1150|James Glasgow]], the documented Edinburgh weaver and burgess, is probably the father. He was admitted burgess in 1649 and was still acting as a weaver, burgess and apprenticeship master in 1693. The published register also places a Robert, son of James Glasgow, weaver, in an apprenticeship in 1672 and a Thomas, youngest son of James Glasgow, weaver and burgess, in one in 1699. This is a coherent later-child group around the same burgh craftsman, but neither the 1696 nor 1699 entry names a mother. The father attachment should remain uncertain pending a baptism, testament or incorporation record with a second identifier.

This James is not the 1690 apprentice, whose father was explicitly deceased. [[Glasgow-1376|James Glasgow]] is excluded because his former 1657 birth was a record-role error based on Marion Glasgow's baptism and his remaining identity has no apothecary-apprenticeship evidence.

'''James Glasgow''' was probably born about 1674. This is an uncertain estimate from his entry into an apprenticeship in 1690; his age was not recorded. His birthplace is unknown. Lindsayland in Biggar parish is usable only as an uncertain location inferred from his father's stated residence.

On 7 May 1690 James, son of the deceased James Glasgow, weaver in Lindsayland, was entered as apprentice to William Brown, a cordiner and tanner in Portsburgh and an Edinburgh burgess. The entry was scored out.<ref name="Apprentice1690">Henry Paton, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/edinburgh_apprentices_~_1666_to_1700_~_1929.pdf ''Register of Apprentices of the City of Edinburgh, 1666–1700''] (Scottish Record Society, 1929), printed p. 37, entry dated 7 May 1690; see also Findmypast, [https://www.findmypast.co.uk/transcript?id=SCOT%2FEDINBURGH%2FAPPRENTICES%2F0005159%2F1&tab=this transcript SCOT/EDINBURGH/APPRENTICES/0005159/1], captured 3 September 2026.</ref>

The scoring-out shows that this apprenticeship was cancelled or did not proceed in its entered form. It does not show that James died.

== Research Notes ==

The father is probably the James Glasgow, weaver at Back of Lindsaylands, whose testament was registered in the Lanark Commissary Court on 10 November 1680.<ref>Francis J. Grant, ed., [https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/the_commissariot_record_of_lanark__register_of_testaments_1595-1800_~_1903.pdf ''The Commissariot Record of Lanark: Register of Testaments, 1595–1800''] (Scottish Record Society, 1903), printed p. 38.</ref> The exact name, occupation, distinctive locality and prior death make that documentary identity strong, but the testament must be inspected before attaching a profile or naming the apprentice's mother.

This James is not the apprentice entered in 1696: the 1690 father was already dead, whereas the 1696 father was a living weaver and burgess. [[Glasgow-3076|James Glasgow]], born at Edinburgh in 1661, is excluded because his profile supplies no Lindsayland or correct-father bridge and he would have been unusually old for this entry.

== Biography ==
{{Notables Sticker}}
James Glasgow was born before 1657, the son of [[Glasgow-1150|James Glasgow]] and [[Duncan-16106|Agnes Duncan]].<ref name=Birth>"Scotland, Births and Baptisms, 1564-1950", database, FamilySearch (https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1YD-PRL : 11 February 2020), James Glesgow in entry for Marione Glesgow, 1657.</ref> He is noted in records during the tumultuous era of the Covenanter movement in Scotland.

In 1670, James appeared in legal proceedings for refusing to give his oath—a requirement aimed at suppressing illegal religious gatherings, known as field conventicles. These conventicles were organized by Presbyterians protesting government-imposed religious uniformity. James is specifically mentioned as being from a place called '''Whitecastle''', a site associated with Covenanting activities, although its exact location remains uncertain.<ref>Wodrow, Robert. ''The History of the Sufferings of the Church of Scotland from the Restoration to the Revolution.'' 1721. [https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-history-of-the-suffe_wodrow-robert_1721_1/page/n795/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 Internet Archive]</ref>

=== Whitecastle and Covenanting Context ===
It is not clear which Whitecastle James was associated with, as many areas in 17th-century Scotland hosted field conventicles, especially in Lanarkshire and Dumfriesshire. Lanarkshire, in particular, was a stronghold of Presbyterian dissent during this period. The fragmentary nature of the source makes it difficult to identify Whitecastle precisely without further geographical or archival clues.

=== Mr. Duncan and 1671 Proceedings ===
References to a certain '''Mr. Duncan''' in July 1671 connect him to the King’s Advocate and to legal action related to nonconformist religious practices. The records do not clarify whether he was a landowner, minister, or another figure who supported or harbored Covenanters. Many individuals, including local gentry and ministers, were penalized for enabling or attending these conventicles.

== Research Notes ==
* '''James Glasgow''' (b. ~late 1600s – d. unknown) may have held a position at Edinburgh Castle in 1738, as mentioned in ''The Principal Acts of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland.''<ref>[https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-principal-acts-of-th_church-of-scotland-gene_1738/page/n19/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 ''The Principal Acts of the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland''], 1738 (Internet Archive)</ref>
* '''James Glasgow''' was a notable figure mentioned in legal proceedings during the turbulent times of the Covenanter movement in Scotland. In July 1670, he was fined for refusing to give his oath, alongside several others, as part of a crackdown on illegal religious gatherings known as field conventicles. These gatherings were a form of protest against the government's attempt to impose religious uniformity, particularly on those who adhered to Presbyterianism. James Glasgow is specifically noted as being from Whitecastle, a location associated with Covenanting activities during this period.<ref>[https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-history-of-the-state_crookshank-william_1751_1/page/284/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 ''The History of the Sufferings of the Church of Scotland from the Restoration to the Revolution''], by Robert Wodrow, 1721</ref>
**From the information provided in the images and context, '''Whitecastle''' is likely a location associated with the '''Covenanter''' activities, but the specific reference does not immediately clarify which Whitecastle it is. Given the widespread nature of the Covenanter movement in '''Scotland''', '''Whitecastle''' could plausibly be located in '''Lanarkshire''', '''Dumfriesshire''', or nearby areas known for strong Covenanter sympathies during the 17th century. The '''Lanarkshire''' region, specifically, was a hotspot for religious dissent during the Covenanting times, making it a strong candidate. However, without further geographic markers or historical maps, it's challenging to conclusively identify Whitecastle's exact location just from this.
**As for '''Mr. Duncan''', the mention of his name in the July 1671 proceedings involving the '''King's Advocate''' seems to tie him to some legal action related to the suppression of religious activities or nonconformity in religious practices. Without more context from the previous or following sections of the document, it's difficult to determine exactly who '''Mr. Duncan''' was. He could have been a local landowner, minister, or someone involved in harboring or protecting Covenanters, as many individuals were targeted during this period for their association with field conventicles.
**Further research into legal records or historical sources about '''Mr. Duncan''' in 1671 and '''Whitecastle''' in Covenanting Scotland would be required to offer a more precise identification.  Note, could be any of the other James Glasgow's in this timespan. No good match for location (Whitecastle) 
* On October 11, 1680, a James Glasgow is listed as a weaver in the Back of Lindsaylands, Parish of Biggar (Lanark Commissary Court, CC14/5/10). It is unclear if he is the same individual.

=== Current research ===

The asserted 29 January 1657 birth and placement as a son of James Glasgow and Agnes Duncan are unsupported and result from a record-role error. The profile's cited FamilySearch entry is for '''Marione Glesgow'''; "James Glesgow" appears in it as her father. It is not a baptism or birth record for a son James.

Glasgow-1376 was previously attached to the household. That relationship has been removed and should not be restored unless an independent record for a son James is found. The profile does not merge this profile into the father merely from the misread citation, because its later Whitecastle/Covenanter claims have not been shown to describe the Edinburgh weaver.

The proposed merge with [[Glasgow-2682|Glasgow-2682]] is also rejected. Glasgow-2682 is a documented father with Isobell Duffe from 1677 to 1691. The false 1657 birth on this profile supplies no matching identity fact, and no record connects the Whitecastle occurrence to the Duffe household.

This assessment draws on the cited records and public source material.<ref name="ProjectSource1">[https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1YD-PRL FamilySearch index X1YD-PRL].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource2">[https://familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:X1YD-PR2 FamilySearch index X1YD-PR2].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource3">[https://www.tradeshouselibrary.org/uploads/4/7/7/2/47723681/roll_of_edinburgh_burgesses_1406_to_1700.pdf#page=101 PDF p. 101].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource4">[https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-history-of-the-suffe_wodrow-robert_1721_1/page/n795/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 archive.org].</ref><ref name="ProjectSource5">[https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-principal-acts-of-th_church-of-scotland-gene_1738/page/n19/mode/2up?q=%22James+Glasgow%22 archive.org].</ref>

The parentage and birth date for James Glasgow are not yet known. Based on the birth of his first known child in 1677, he was likely born by about 1657.

He was married to [[Duffe-18|Isobell Duffe]]. Her name is recorded as "Issobell Duff" or "Issobell Duffe" in the christening records of most of their children.

James and Issobell had the following children, all christened in Edinburgh Parish, Midlothian, Scotland:

== Research Notes ==
'''Identifying the parents of James Glasgow is a top research priority.''' Several contemporary men named James Glasgow who were also having children in Edinburgh at the same time have been investigated and ruled out as being the same person, though they are likely relatives (e.g., brothers or cousins). These include:
*   '''[[Glasgow-3098|James Glasgow (b. 1631)]]''', who was married to Bessie Whyte.
*   '''[[Glasgow-3077|James Glasgow (b. bef. 1640)]]''', who was married to Helen Clerk.
*   '''[[Glasgow-3337|James Glasgow (b. ca. 1640)]]''', who was married to Annapill Glessie.

Since our James was consistently recorded with his wife, [[Duffe-18|Isobell Duffe]], it is highly unlikely he is the same person as any of the men listed above.

*   '''Parentage is Unknown:''' The parents of James are not yet confirmed. The original profile suggested he might descend from the Midlothian line of [[Glasgow-1168|James Glasgow (abt.1540-1580)]], perhaps as a son of [[Glasgow-1151|Johne Glasgow (1632-)]] or [[Glasgow-1084|John Glasgow (bef.1616-)]]. This is speculative and requires further research to find a primary source linking him to a father.
*   '''Conflicting Mother's Name:''' The 1679 christening record for his son [[Glasgow-3103|James]] lists the mother's name as "Elizabeth Duffe" instead of "Issobell". As all other children's records name her as Issobell, and given the commonality of clerical errors, it is most likely that "Elizabeth" was a mistake by the parish clerk.
*   '''Future Research:''' The highest priority is to find a marriage record for James Glasgow and Issobell Duffe in the Edinburgh parish registers, likely dated before April 1677. A search for burial records for both James and Issobell after March 1691 should also be conducted.
